hints: An address has exactly 4 parts, each 1 to 3 digits. How few choices does that leave at each step, and which parts are clearly illegal?

Backtrack over the 4 parts. For each part try lengths 1, 2, 3; reject a part with a leading zero (length > 1 starting with 0) or a value above 255. Prune when the remaining digits can't fill the remaining parts (need between 1× and 3× parts left).

1. go(pos, parts) where parts holds the numbers chosen so far.
  2. If 4 parts are chosen: save join(".") only if pos == n.
  3. If the digits left are fewer than parts left, or more than 3× parts left, return.
  4. For length 1..3: take the piece; skip it if it has a leading zero or is > 255.
  5. Add the piece, recurse with pos + len, remove it.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every way to place 3 dots (choose 3 of n-1 gaps) and validate the 4 numbers.

approaches.name: Optimal: backtracking over 4 parts with pruning
approaches.idea: At most 3 choices per part and only 4 parts, so at most 3<sup>4</sup> = 81 branches regardless of the input.
approaches.time: O(1) (at most 81 leaves, each O(n) to build)

explain: For "19216811" (8 digits) the first part can be 1, 19 or 192. Following 192, then 168, the last 2 digits must split as 1.1, giving 192.168.1.1. Parts like 921 or 681 are rejected for exceeding 255, which is how we end with 9 addresses. For "1010" only 1.0.1.0 works, since 01 and 010 are blocked by the leading-zero rule. A string longer than 12 digits gives no answer at all.
recognize: 'Insert separators so every segment is valid, return all ways' with a fixed small number of segments → bounded backtracking with validity pruning.
